## Why this matters

Tree-based methods dominate applied machine learning on tabular data, and for good
reasons: they need no scaling, handle mixed variable types, find interactions without
being told, and cope with non-linearity by construction. In marine work they are the
default choice for habitat models and species distribution models.

They also invite a specific mistake — assuming that the more elaborate member of the
family is the better one. This page fits all three on the same survey and the ranking
is the reverse of the reputation.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The idea

### A single decision tree

A tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions. *Is depth below 97 m? If yes, is temperature
above 7.4 °C?* Each answer sends the station down a branch, and the prediction is the
average of the training stations that ended in the same leaf.

Fitting is greedy. At each node the algorithm tries every split of every variable and
keeps the one that most reduces error, then repeats inside each side. It never revisits
an earlier choice.

The appeal is that you can read it. A tree is the only non-linear model in this course
you can print and hand to a colleague who does not model.

### Random forest

A single tree is unstable: change a few stations and the first split may change, and
everything below it with it. Random forests exploit that instability instead of
fighting it.

Build hundreds of trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the rows, and at each split
consider only a random subset of the variables. Individually these trees are worse than
one carefully fitted tree. Averaged, they are usually much better, because their errors
are partly independent and averaging cancels them.

The forced random subset of variables is the part people find counter-intuitive. Without
it, every tree would begin with the same dominant variable and the trees would be too
similar to benefit from averaging.

### Boosting

Boosting builds trees in sequence, each one fitting what the previous ones got wrong.
Trees are small — often only a few splits — and each contributes a fraction of its
prediction, set by the **learning rate**.

This is the most powerful of the three on most benchmarks and the least forgiving. A
forest with too many trees is merely slow; a boosted model with too many trees fits the
noise, and it does so smoothly enough that nothing looks wrong until you check on held-out
data.

## Worked example

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
  salinity_psu + substrate + season

base_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors())

dummied_recipe <- base_recipe |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
```

### A tree you can read

```{r}
#| label: fig-tree
#| fig-cap: "A depth-3 regression tree for abundance. Each box shows the predicted count, the number of training stations reaching it, and their percentage of the total. The root splits on chlorophyll; the low-chlorophyll branch then carves out a temperature band."
#| fig-alt: "A decision tree diagram three levels deep. The root splits on chlorophyll below 1.7. The low-chlorophyll branch, holding 76 percent of stations, splits on temperature below 6.4 and then on temperature at or above 11, isolating a middle band predicting 4.2 individuals against 1.4 for cold water and 2.1 for warm. The high-chlorophyll branch splits again on chlorophyll and on substrate, reaching leaves predicting up to 19 individuals from 3 stations. Depth does not appear anywhere in the tree."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
tree_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(base_recipe) |>
  add_model(decision_tree(tree_depth = 3, min_n = 5) |>
              set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression")) |>
  fit(train)

rpart.plot(extract_fit_engine(tree_fit),
           roundint = FALSE, type = 2, extra = 101,
           box.palette = "Blues", branch.lty = 3, cex = 0.8)
```

Read the left branch, which holds three-quarters of the stations. Below 6.4 °C the model
expects 1.4 individuals. At or above 11 °C it expects 2.1. In between — 6.4 to 11 °C — it
expects 4.2. The tree has carved out a temperature band, and the simulation's true
optimum of 9 °C sits inside it.

That is worth pausing on, because it shows how a tree represents an optimum. A single
threshold cannot express "best in the middle"; it takes **two splits at the same level**,
one cutting off each tail. Anything hump-shaped costs a tree twice what a monotonic
relationship costs.

Which explains the surprise at the root. The strongest effects in the simulation are the
depth and temperature optima, yet the first split is on **chlorophyll**, and depth does
not appear anywhere in three levels. Chlorophyll's effect is monotonic — more is better —
so one threshold captures a good share of it, while depth needs two splits before it
pays anything at all. A greedy algorithm that takes the best single split at each step is
systematically biased towards monotonic predictors.

::: {.callout-note}
A variable's absence from a tree is not evidence that it does not matter. Depth is one of
the two strongest drivers in this dataset by construction, and it is missing here because
its effect is hump-shaped and partly carried by temperature, which is itself a function
of depth. Read tree structure as *one* account of the data, not *the* account.
:::

The cost of this legibility is that the thresholds are arbitrary. There is nothing
biological about 1.7 mg m⁻³; it is where this particular sample happened to split best,
and another survey would give a different number.

### All three, side by side

```{r}
#| label: compare-three
evaluate <- function(model, recipe, label) {
  fitted <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe) |> add_model(model) |> fit(train)
  tibble(
    model      = label,
    train_rmse = round(as.numeric(rmse(augment(fitted, train), abundance, .pred)$.estimate), 2),
    test_rmse  = round(as.numeric(rmse(augment(fitted, test), abundance, .pred)$.estimate), 2),
    test_rsq   = round(as.numeric(rsq(augment(fitted, test), abundance, .pred)$.estimate), 3)
  )
}

bind_rows(
  evaluate(decision_tree(tree_depth = 3, min_n = 5) |> set_engine("rpart") |>
             set_mode("regression"), base_recipe, "Tree (depth 3)"),
  evaluate(decision_tree() |> set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression"),
           base_recipe, "Tree (defaults)"),
  evaluate(rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 9) |>
             set_mode("regression"), base_recipe, "Random forest (500)"),
  evaluate(boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.1, tree_depth = 4) |>
             set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("regression"),
           dummied_recipe, "Boosting (500 trees)")
)
```

The ordering deserves a moment. **Both single trees beat both ensembles.** The two trees
come in at 4.76 and 4.81 — close enough to be indistinguishable on 200 test stations —
the random forest is behind them at 4.84, and the 500-tree boosted model is worst by a
wide margin.

Now read the training column alongside it. Boosting fits its training data to an RMSE of
0.58, roughly seven times better than the trees manage, and predicts new stations worst
of all. That pair of numbers — 0.58 against 5.49 — is the whole story.

### Watching it happen

```{r}
#| label: fig-capacity
#| fig-cap: "Error against model capacity, on training data and on held-out data. Both methods fit the training data better and better as they grow. Both predict new stations worse after a point — boosting after about 50 trees, the tree after depth 3. The gap that opens between the two lines is overfitting, made visible."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels, each with two lines. Left, boosting: training RMSE falls steadily from about 4 to near zero as trees increase from 5 to 800, while test RMSE dips slightly to about 5.1 at 50 trees then rises to 5.5. Right, tree depth: training RMSE falls from 4.3 to 3.4 as depth increases from 1 to 8, while test RMSE falls to 4.8 at depth 3 then rises to 5.0."
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
boosting_curve <- map(c(5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800), \(n) {
  fitted <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(dummied_recipe) |>
    add_model(boost_tree(trees = n, learn_rate = 0.1, tree_depth = 4) |>
                set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("regression")) |>
    fit(train)
  tibble(capacity = n,
         Training = as.numeric(rmse(augment(fitted, train), abundance, .pred)$.estimate),
         `Held-out` = as.numeric(rmse(augment(fitted, test), abundance, .pred)$.estimate))
}) |> list_rbind() |> pivot_longer(-capacity, names_to = "data", values_to = "rmse")

depth_curve <- map(1:8, \(d) {
  fitted <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(base_recipe) |>
    add_model(decision_tree(tree_depth = d, min_n = 5) |>
                set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression")) |>
    fit(train)
  tibble(capacity = d,
         Training = as.numeric(rmse(augment(fitted, train), abundance, .pred)$.estimate),
         `Held-out` = as.numeric(rmse(augment(fitted, test), abundance, .pred)$.estimate))
}) |> list_rbind() |> pivot_longer(-capacity, names_to = "data", values_to = "rmse")

p_boost <- ggplot(boosting_curve, aes(capacity, rmse, colour = data)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of trees (log scale)", y = "RMSE", colour = NULL,
       title = "Boosting")

p_depth <- ggplot(depth_curve, aes(capacity, rmse, colour = data)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  labs(x = "Tree depth", y = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "A single tree")

p_boost + p_depth + plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## What the results mean

Two lessons, and the second is the transferable one.

**More capacity is not more skill.** With about 600 training stations and genuinely noisy
counts, there is only so much signal available. Past that point, extra flexibility
learns the particular stations in this survey. The tree bottoms out at depth 3; boosting
at roughly 50 trees.

**Boosting's defaults are not safe defaults.** A random forest with too many trees costs
computing time. Boosting with too many trees costs accuracy, and the damage is invisible
without held-out data. Boosting must be tuned —
[section 5](../05-generalisation/index.qmd) covers how — and an untuned boosted model is
not evidence about boosting.

It is worth saying plainly that this ordering is a fact about *this dataset*, not a
general ranking. With 50,000 rows and a strong signal, boosting would very likely win.
The general claim is narrower and more useful: **the amount of flexibility you can
afford is set by how much data and how much signal you have**, and neither is under your
control.

## Where this breaks down

**Trees cannot extrapolate. At all.** A tree's prediction is the mean of training
stations in a leaf, so beyond the range of the training data the prediction is flat —
constant, forever. A forest of trees is still flat. For predicting into warmer water
than you have sampled, this is not conservatism; it is a model asserting no change with
complete confidence. [Section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd) returns to
this, and it is a strong argument for a parametric model when extrapolation is the point.

**A single tree is unstable.** Refit on a bootstrap sample and the splits move. Do not
over-interpret a specific threshold, and be wary of a paper that does.

**Forests and boosting are not interpretable** in the way the printed tree is. Variable
importance is available ([section 10](../10-interpretation/index.qmd)) and it is a much
weaker thing than a set of readable rules.

**Greedy splitting is biased towards monotonic variables.** As above, a hump-shaped
driver has to buy two splits before it earns anything, so it can lose to a weaker but
monotonic competitor and vanish from the tree entirely.

**Trees handle interactions but hide them.** The structure encodes interactions
implicitly; nothing reports "depth and temperature interact". You have to go looking.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- A tree is a sequence of yes/no splits, and it is the only non-linear model here you
  can print and read.
- A tree needs two splits to express an optimum, so it favours monotonic predictors. Here
  depth — a real driver — never appears, while chlorophyll takes the root.
- A random forest averages many deliberately varied trees; the random subset of
  variables at each split is what makes averaging pay.
- Boosting fits trees in sequence to the previous trees' errors. It is the strongest and
  the least forgiving, and it needs tuning rather than defaults.
- On this survey, both single trees beat both ensembles. With ~600 noisy rows there is
  not enough signal to pay for more flexibility.
- Training error falling while held-out error rises is overfitting. Boosting reached a
  training RMSE of 0.58 against a test RMSE of 5.49.
- Trees cannot extrapolate. Outside the sampled range their predictions are flat and
  confident.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Refit the depth-3 tree on three bootstrap samples of the training data and compare
   the root split each time. Is it always chlorophyll, and is the threshold stable?
2. Set `learn_rate = 0.01` in the 500-tree boosted model. Does slowing the learning
   rate recover the performance that 500 trees lost, and what does that suggest about
   which knob matters?
